newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Mostar investigation blames Bosnian Croat police.
newsitem.headline: Mostar investigation blames Bosnian Croat police.

text.p: International police investigators reported on Tuesday that Bosnian Croat police fired on unarmed Moslems without cause and behaved in a criminal manner in an incident this month in the divided town of Mostar.

"The use by law enforcement officers of excessive force in beating marchers, and of unnecessary and disproportionate lethal force, resulted in one death and numerous injuries," said the international police report, obtained by Reuters.

The investigation, conducted by a team of monitors from the International Police Task Force (IPTF), said two Croat police were photographed firing into a crowd of retreating Moslems who had tried to visit a cemetery in Croat-held western Mostar.
One of the policeman was identified as Ivan Hrkac, deputy chief of police in western Mostar, the report said.
Witnesses said a third policeman in plain clothes was seen firing into the crowd. Three other policemen were photographed with their weapons drawn, according to the report.
The February 10 attack, which left one Moslem man dead and at least 20 wounded, marked the most serious violence to erupt in Bosnia since a peace agreement was signed in December 1995.
Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia, met leaders of the Moslem-Croat federation on Tuesday evening to discuss the IPTF report.

The investigation concluded that the Croat police had been informed beforehand about the planned procession and had assigned police to the route near the Liska cemetery, where Moslems and Croats are buried side by side.

After the incident, Croat police launched a "concerted effort" to cover-up the facts of the attack, with Croat police chief Marko Radic and other officers presenting false information to IPTF investigators, the report said.
Their behaviour "reflects the absence of professional leadership at the highest level in the west Mostar police", it said.
The report dismissed previous allegations in the Croat media that the Moslems had staged the procession in an attempt to provoke a confrontation with a carnival celebration on the same day.
The carnival was held "several blocks away" from the procession route, the report said.
Diplomats said the report, which did not shy away from pinning blame on the Croat police, placed Western envoys and the NATO-led police force in a difficult position.
"The report is very solid. But what's the next step? Who will arrest the accused?" said one diplomat, who asked not to be named.
Previous demands by international officials for Croat authorities to punish those responsible for abuses have failed in the past to produce results.

By clearly naming the culprits, the international community risked losing credibility among the former warring factions if it failed to ensure that perpretrators were brought to justice, the diplomat said.
Croat authorities have suspended six policemen over the incident but have also pressed charges against Moslems for allegedly provoking the violence.
The Croat interior minister for the county said on Monday he had launched legal proceedings for the removal of his Moslem deputy, Sefkija Dziha, the Croatian state news agency HINA reported.
Violence in Mostar has damaged already strained relations within the Moslem-Croat federation, which together with the Serb republic comprises peacetime Bosnia.
